title: Building a MaaS App: GTFS, GBFS, Taxi Integration and Fare Capping
summary:
Quick Answer

A Mobility as a Service (MaaS) app combines public transit, taxis, ride-hailing, bike share and scooters into one trip planner with one account. Technically, it is an integration project: you consume open data feeds such as GTFS, GTFS-Realtime and GBFS, connect booking APIs from taxi and on-demand operators, and wrap everything in a routing engine and a single payment layer. The hardest parts are data quality, real-time accuracy and fare logic, not the mobile UI.

What data feeds does a MaaS app need?

Most of the open mobility data you need already exists in standard formats:

  • GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification): static schedules, stops, routes and fares for public transit.
  • GTFS-Realtime: live vehicle positions, trip updates and service alerts, usually as Protocol Buffers.
  • GBFS (General Bikeshare Feed Specification): station status, free-floating vehicle locations and availability for bikes and scooters.
  • Operator APIs: booking, pricing and ETA endpoints for taxi fleets, ride-hailing partners and microtransit services.

A practical tip: treat every feed as unreliable. Validate it on ingest, keep the last good version, and alert when a feed goes stale. A trip planner that suggests a bus that stopped running yesterday loses trust immediately.

How does multimodal routing work?

The core of a MaaS app is a routing engine that can combine walking, transit, bikes and car trips. Open-source engines such as OpenTripPlanner are widely used because they understand GTFS and GBFS natively. A typical flow looks like this:

  1. The rider enters origin, destination and departure or arrival time.
  2. The engine builds candidate itineraries across modes.
  3. Real-time data adjusts arrival predictions and removes cancelled trips.
  4. Itineraries are ranked by time, cost, transfers and walking distance.
  5. On-demand legs, such as a taxi for the last mile, are priced live through operator APIs.

The trick is combining scheduled and on-demand legs. A taxi ETA changes minute by minute, while a train follows a timetable, so the app needs to re-check on-demand availability before the rider commits.

Where does the taxi integration fit?

Taxi and ride-hailing legs are what make MaaS useful outside dense transit areas. The integration usually needs:

  • Real-time availability and ETA by location
  • Upfront fare quotes or fare estimates
  • Booking, cancellation and status webhooks
  • Driver location updates during the trip
  • Payment handled through the MaaS account, with settlement to the operator

If you are building the taxi side yourself, the dispatch system matters more than the rider screens. Teams working on taxi booking app development often expose a clean partner API from day one, because it lets the fleet join MaaS platforms, corporate travel tools and hotel concierge systems without separate integrations.

How do you handle payments and fares?

One account, one payment method and one receipt is the promise of MaaS. Behind it, the platform needs:

  • Account-based ticketing: the rider's account, not a physical card, holds entitlements.
  • Fare capping: frequent riders never pay more than a daily, weekly or monthly limit.
  • Split settlement: revenue from a combined trip is shared correctly between operators.
  • Concessions: discounted fares for students, seniors or low-income riders, verified once and applied automatically.

Fare rules differ by agency and change over time, so model them as configuration, not code.

What are the hard engineering problems?

  • Data freshness: real-time feeds drop or lag; the app must degrade gracefully.
  • Identity across operators: one rider may need accounts or tokens with several partners.
  • Offline use: riders lose signal underground, so tickets and itineraries should work offline.
  • Accessibility: step-free routes, wheelchair-accessible vehicles and screen reader support are essential, especially for public-sector clients.
  • Privacy: trip histories reveal where people live and work; minimize what you store and how long you keep it.

Who usually buys a MaaS platform?

In the US, MaaS projects often start with a city, a regional transit agency, a university campus or a large employer, rather than a consumer startup. That affects scope: procurement requirements, accessibility standards and data-sharing agreements can take as long as the build itself. Anyone planning MaaS solutions should budget for open data standards, open APIs and clear reporting, because public partners expect them.

A minimal architecture

  • Ingestion services for GTFS, GTFS-Realtime and GBFS, with validation and versioning
  • Routing engine (for example, OpenTripPlanner) with real-time updates
  • Partner gateway for taxi, ride-hailing and microtransit APIs
  • Account and payments service with fare capping and settlement
  • Mobile apps with offline tickets, live trip tracking and accessibility settings
  • Operator dashboard for service alerts, analytics and reporting

Final thoughts

MaaS succeeds when the data underneath is trustworthy and the payment experience feels like one product. Start with reliable feeds and one or two partner integrations, prove that riders complete trips end to end, and expand modes and partners from there.

title: Don't let your agents' dreams turn into nightmares. Let them daydream.
summary:
Agent memory had a busy year. The newest trick is dreaming: a background job that, between sessions, reads back through an agent's logs and rewrites its memory. It merges duplicates, corrects notes it thinks are wrong, and promotes the important ones into the context the next session starts with. Anthropic described it this month as offline reflection on logs, named after the way the hippocampus replays the day while you sleep (https://anthropic.com/research/components-of-agent-memory).
I build OmniMem (https://github.com/richarvey/OmniMem), an open source memory server for AI agents, written in Rust and served over MCP. Dreaming tackles the problem I care about most: agents that never learn from their own sessions. But the way it's usually built, unattended and in the background, runs straight into something we learned the hard way with production systems. State that changes without a gate eventually changes in a way you didn't want.
This post is the argument for manual gates on agent memory, what OmniMem already gates, and how 7.2 adds learning from session transcripts, which I'm calling daydreaming, without giving up any of them.

The criticism, and the gate that answers it

In August The New Stack collected practitioners' reactions to dreaming (https://thenewstack.io/anthropic-agent-memory-dreaming/). In fairness, Anthropic's own talk sent proposed updates to a human for review. The critics' point was that this isn't enough on its own. Here's what they raised, paraphrased, with what OmniMem does about each.

  • Repeated mistakes get promoted to permanent policy, and review becomes a rubber stamp at fleet scale (Jayakumar Ramalingam). In OmniMem nothing becomes a skill or a believed memory without a person accepting it, one item at a time, and proposals carry the memories they came from.- "The right instinct aimed at the wrong evidence", and a store that drifts towards whatever happened lately (Vladimir Beskorovainyi). Daydream's reinforcement gate counts sessions across the whole history, not the latest batch.- Transcripts hold content the agent never wrote, so an automated writer reading them is an attack surface (Viktor Bulanek). The detectors are deterministic pattern matchers, not a model. Transcripts pass the scrub gate first, and every finding waits for a person.- A persisted hallucination becomes infrastructure; provenance matters, and sometimes forgetting is the safe move (Berk Yilmaz). Every memory carries provenance and validity dates, there are tools to end a fact's validity or forget it, and contradiction resolution keeps the losing side for audit.- Dreaming isn't cheap or deterministic like garbage collection; it's repeated paid model runs (Kerstin Frailey). Detection and the skill compiler are deterministic and local. An LLM is optional and only rewords a proposal.The common thread: memory is state that agents act on, so every change to it needs evidence, an owner and a way back. ## What OmniMem already gates (7.0.x, today) None of this is new for 7.2. It's the foundation daydreaming sits on, and it's why I didn't want to bolt on an unattended loop.
  • Skills: propose, then a person accepts. compile_skill in propose mode turns accumulated experience into a SKILL.md draft and returns a diff. Write mode is only a request: by default (HUMAN_APPROVAL=human) OmniMem asks the person through MCP elicitation, or parks the proposal in the settings panel's Pending list when the client can't ask. The compiler is deterministic, so the same sources render a byte-identical skill and a diff only ever shows a real change.- Trust: only a person moves it. Every memory has a trust state: candidate, accepted, disputed, superseded or rejected. Facts the enrichment worker extracts start as candidates. Confirming or rejecting goes through the panel or the CLI, and there is deliberately no MCP tool that can do it. Restoring a backup never raises trust either, so a doctored backup can't promote anything.- Contradictions: resolved, never deleted. check_contradictions links memories that disagree. Its resolve mode records the outcome on both sides and goes through the same human approval as skills. The loser is kept with the reason, and the decision can be reopened.- Provenance and licence on every memory. Retrieved (an outside source), concluded (the system's own reasoning) or asserted (you said it), decided at write time and never scored on.- Time. Memories carry valid_from and valid_to, end_validity closes a fact that stopped being true, and recall accepts valid_at and known_at, so you can ask what was true in March and what OmniMem believed at the time.- Audit. The store writes the audit log in the same transaction as the change. Below the full level no row holds memory text, and a forget scrubs earlier rows for that memory too.- The graveyard. record_experience and log_abandoned record approaches that failed and why. A PreToolUse hook (Claude Code, OpenCode, the Mistral Vibe CLI and Kiro) refuses a tool call that repeats a known dead end. On my dead-end benchmark that hook was the difference: agents with the answer already in the store made no memory calls on their own.## Daydream: learning from transcripts, with you in the room The gap all those gates left: OmniMem only learned from what an agent chose to remember, and agents mostly don't choose. The session transcript is the best record of what really happened, and OmniMem never read it. 7.2 changes that, and it's in development now on the v7.2.x branch. When it runs. Only when a person is there: importing a log, a session-end hook firing, or pressing Daydream now. There is no scheduler. Where the logs come from. Five routes feed one pipeline: the desktop app (local discovery and a local scan), the settings panel's new Logs page (browser upload), omnimem logs import on the CLI, session-end hooks, and a new MCP tool, submit_session_log, for clients that keep no transcripts locally. That's the 50th tool. Day one covers every client OmniMem has a guide for:
  • Read from disk: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot (VS Code), Kiro, Mistral Vibe CLI, OpenCode- Account export upload: claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Mistral Vibe on the web (formerly Le Chat)- Agent submits its own session: GitLab Duo, Lumo, Open Design*What it looks for.* Seven deterministic detectors: tool_error, retry_loop, user_correction, revert, abandoned, recovery and guard_hit. A failure followed by a recovery becomes a proposed piece of experience: the approach that failed, and the fix that worked. Repeated failure with no recovery becomes a proposed dead end. Repeated corrections on one topic become a candidate preference, in your own words. When it proposes. A signal has to recur in at least two distinct sessions, counted across the whole history, before anything is proposed. A pattern seen in one client only stays scoped to that client, which is also the evidence the model-routing work planned for 7.3 will need. Where it lands. As a candidate, with the client, the model and references back to the sessions and turns it came from. It goes into the Pending list. Nothing daydreamed is ever accepted without a person. The defaults change nothing until you import a log: DAYDREAM=manual, DAYDREAM_MIN_SESSIONS=2, DAYDREAM_LLM=off and TRANSCRIPT_RETENTION=none. ## The scrub gate: no secrets reach an LLM Transcripts are where credentials leak: the .env an agent prints, the token in a curl command, the connection string in a stack trace. A memory store is the worst place for one, because recall will put it straight back into a later session's context, and from there into a model provider's request log. ### Where 7.0 was 7.0's Claude Code session-end hook already redacted its session record with a redact() function: seven regexes, compiled on every call. It caught OpenAI-style sk- keys, GitHub tokens, AWS access key IDs, bearer tokens, password= style assignments, PEM private keys and JWTs. It missed GitLab and Slack tokens, Google keys, Tailscale keys and passwords inside database URLs. And nothing stopped a future code path skipping it. ### What 7.2 does instead A new crate, omnimem-scrub, sits in front of everything, and the core idea is to make skipping it impossible to compile. Text straight from a transcript is a RawText: no Display, no Serialize, and a Debug that prints a placeholder. The only way to get a CleanText is Scrubber::scan(), which fails closed. The store, the embedder, the LLM client and the queue take CleanText only. Forgetting to scan stops being a bug you find in production and becomes a build that won't compile. The rules run in layers:
  • Known formats: provider and platform tokens (Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Stripe, Google, Tailscale, Cloudflare, Hugging Face, npm, PyPI), PEM keys, JWTs, and OmniMem's own bearer and OAuth secrets- Credentials in structure: passwords in URLs, Authorization and Cookie headers, .env blocks, password flags- Keyword plus entropy: a high-entropy value next to secret, token or api_key, the way gitleaks does it, which catches formats nobody listed- Your own secrets by fingerprint: register a token or a config file and OmniMem keeps a salted SHA-256 and a length, never the value- Personal data, opt-in: emails, phone numbers, private IPs, tailnet hostnamesThe built-in pack is written in gitleaks' TOML rule format, so you can drop in an existing gitleaks.toml. A hit becomes a typed placeholder carrying a short keyed hash, so the same secret gets the same placeholder throughout a session and "the key that failed" still makes sense to a detector, but the value is never recoverable. Rules marked as blocking, like private keys, drop the whole turn, and too many in one session quarantine it for review. The crate also builds for WebAssembly, so the settings panel scans a log in your browser before upload, and the server scans it again on arrival. The findings report holds counts and offsets, never values. With the default retention, no transcript text is stored at all. The tests are the part I'll hold the release on. A canary test plants fake secrets of every rule type in every adapter's fixtures, runs a full import and daydream, then byte-searches the database, the WAL, the audit log, captured tracing output, the embedder's inputs and a mocked LLM's request log. One hit fails the build. ## Follow along, or pick something up Dreaming will mature, and plenty of the people building it care about these problems. My position is simple: memory that agents act on should only change when a person says so, with the evidence attached and a way back. Let your agents daydream. Keep the nightmares out. All of 7.2 is public:
  • Milestone 7.2.0, 18 issues starting with the scrub gate: https://github.com/richarvey/OmniMem/milestone/6- Milestone 7.2.1, the follow-ups: https://github.com/richarvey/OmniMem/milestone/7- The scrub gate issue, with the type design: https://github.com/richarvey/OmniMem/issues/44- The spec: https://github.com/richarvey/OmniMem/blob/v7.2.x/docs/daydream-spec.mdIf you know one of these clients' log formats better than its docs do, the adapter issues are a good place to start. And if you think a gate is still too thin, I'd rather hear it now than after release. Reply here, open an issue, or find me on Mastodon at https://mastodon.squarecows.com/@ric

title: The Vault Held. The Roster Didn't: What the 1Password Breach Actually Teaches Builders
summary:
The Vault Held. The Roster Didn't: What the 1Password Breach Actually Teaches Builders

Yesterday, 1Password told the world it had been hacked. By this morning the story was the top post on Hacker News, with over a thousand points and nearly five hundred comments. The headline everywhere was the same: customer data stolen, source code stolen, but your passwords are safe.

All three parts of that headline are true. And the third part, the reassuring one, is exactly why this breach is worth a closer look. Because the vault holding is not the whole story. It never is.

What actually happened

On November 19, 1Password noticed suspicious activity and started investigating. An attacker had gotten into an employee's corporate GitHub account. That is the whole entry point. No zero-day, no exotic exploit chain, just one person's GitHub account.

From there, the attacker did what a compromised GitHub account lets you do at a company that ships code from GitHub: they reached private source code repositories, and they pushed malicious code into backend services. That code downloaded customer account records.

Here is what left the building:

  • Names and email addresses
  • Account and user identifiers, plus account creation and last sign-in times
  • Public keys
  • Secure Remote Password protocol parameters
  • Tokens embedded in emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery
  • Internal metadata, things like version numbers and file identifiers

And here is what did not: no vault content, no passwords, no secrets, no vault items, no account recovery keys, and none of the keys that protect the vaults. 1Password says the vaults were never available to the attacker at any point. The apps and browser extensions are unaffected.

The company also says the stolen email-link tokens cannot be used on their own to get into an account, because finishing an invitation or recovery flow still needs either single sign-on or a verification code sent to the user's email. Only a small number of users were affected by the token part, and those people were notified individually. There is no evidence of any account takeover so far, and independent security experts have been brought in to check the cleanup.

The response was fast and, to be fair, thorough. The compromised GitHub account was disabled, the stolen token revoked, clean versions of the affected services restored, internal credentials rotated, and GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls hardened. As a precaution, the codes in invitation and recovery emails were lengthened from six digits to ten characters.

That is a good incident response. I am going to spend the rest of this article explaining why it still leaves me uneasy, and what I would take from it if I ran a service of my own.

The architecture worked. Say so plainly.

First, credit where it is due. The reason 1Password can say "your passwords are safe" with a straight face is that it built its system so that it cannot read your vaults in the first place. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold. The company cannot access them, which means an attacker who gets into the company's servers cannot either.

That is the whole point of a zero-knowledge design, and this week it did its job under real fire. A lot of companies claim their encryption means even they cannot read your data. Very few of them get a live test of that claim, in public, with the entire internet watching. This one passed.

If you build anything that stores other people's secrets, this is the standard. The question is not whether your servers are hard to break into. The question is what an attacker gets if they succeed anyway. 1Password's answer was: the roster, not the secrets. That distinction is the entire architecture, and it held.

I build a messenger. I think about this question constantly, because my users' messages are the same kind of thing as 1Password's vaults: if my server gets owned, the messages must still be unreadable. That is why the encryption keys live on the devices, not on my server, and why I lose sleep over anything that could quietly move a key to the server side. This week is a reminder that the design choice matters more than any firewall.

But the roster is not nothing

Here is the part that gets lost when everyone repeats "vaults are safe" like a slogan. The attacker walked away with a list of people who use 1Password, their names, their email addresses, and when they last signed in.

That is a phishing list. A good one. Every name on it is a confirmed user of a password manager, which means every name on it is someone who guards accounts worth stealing. The sign-in times tell an attacker who is active. The account creation dates tell them who is new, and new users are the easiest to trick.

1Password knows this, which is why its own advice is to watch for unexpected invitations, recovery requests, and phishing attempts, and why it keeps repeating that it will never contact you to ask for your password or Secret Key. The next wave of this breach will not be a technical attack. It will be emails that look exactly like 1Password, sent to people who now know 1Password was breached, telling them to click a link and fix their account. That is the part of this story that has not happened yet.

There is a lesson here for anyone who builds a service. We spend a lot of time arguing about whether the encrypted payload is safe, and not nearly enough time asking what the metadata is worth. Names, emails, sign-in times, account IDs: none of it is a secret, and all of it is useful to an attacker. When you design your data model, the metadata deserves the same "what if they read it all" treatment as the secrets. Most of the time, it does not get it.

One GitHub account was the whole attack

Step back and look at the shape of this breach. The entry point was a single employee's GitHub account. From that one account, the attacker reached source code, reached the CI/CD system, and pushed code into production backend services.

That is the sentence I keep coming back to. One account, and the blast radius was the build pipeline.

Every company that ships from GitHub has this shape, including mine, including probably yours. A developer's GitHub account is not a code-hosting login. It is a production credential with a friendly interface. It can push code that runs on your servers, read private repositories, and reach the CI/CD system that holds infrastructure secrets. 1Password says it rotated the infrastructure credentials that may have been exposed, which tells you those credentials were reachable from the CI/CD system in the first place.

I am not saying this to scold 1Password. Their GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls have now been hardened, and the compromised account is disabled. I am saying it because the pattern is everywhere, and most teams have not thought about it this way. Ask yourself: if one of your developers' GitHub accounts got taken over tonight, what could the attacker reach before morning? If the honest answer is "the build pipeline and everything behind it," then that account deserves the same protection as your production database credentials. Hardware security keys for GitHub, short-lived tokens, tight repository permissions, and a CI/CD system that cannot push to production on the strength of a single login.

The same week, Todoist reportedly lost a similar fight through a stolen developer credential. Two companies, same shape of failure, same week. That is not a coincidence. It is what happens when an entire industry treats developer accounts as ordinary logins while giving them extraordinary reach.

The code was stolen too, and that matters more than it sounds

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories. 1Password says the source code is not customer data and contains no user secrets, and that there is no impact to services, availability, or product security. That may all be true.

But source code is still a map. It shows an attacker how the system works, where the checks are, what the internal services are called, and what assumptions the developers made. It makes the next attack easier, and it makes the next phishing email more convincing, because the attacker can now write messages that sound like they came from someone who has read the codebase. Source code theft is a slow-burn problem. Its effects show up months later, in attacks that look unrelated.

If you keep secrets out of your source code, good. That is table stakes, and it is the reason 1Password can say the stolen code contains no user secrets. But "no secrets in the code" is not the same as "the code is safe to lose." Treat your private repositories like what they are: a detailed description of your system, written by the people who built it, handed to whoever gets in.

What I am actually doing about this

I am not a 1Password customer writing a breakup letter. I am a developer who runs a small service and reads breach reports the way other people read the weather. Here is what this one changed for me:

Treat every developer account as a production credential. GitHub, the CI system, the cloud console: if it can push code or read infrastructure secrets, it gets hardware-key authentication and the tightest permissions I can give it without breaking the workflow. A password and a phone prompt are not enough for an account that can deploy to production.

Log the reads, not just the writes. The Hex.pm breach earlier this week had the same blind spot I keep seeing in these reports: the team could prove what was changed, but not what was read. If someone pushes code into your backend, you need to know what that code touched. Instrument the sensitive reads now, while nothing is on fire.

Keep the keys on the user's side, and prove it. The one thing 1Password could say with total confidence this week is that the vaults were safe, because the design makes it true even when everything else fails. If you store other people's secrets, build so that a full server compromise still leaves the secrets unreadable. Then say so plainly, and mean it.

Expect the phishing wave, not the technical sequel. The stolen data here is a targeting list. If you run a service and you ever have a breach, your users' inboxes are the second battlefield. Tell them what you will never ask for, in plain language, before the fake emails start arriving.

The uncomfortable summary

1Password's vaults held because the architecture was designed for exactly this day. That is a genuine achievement, and it is the reason this breach is a bad week instead of a catastrophe.

But a single GitHub account opened the door to the source code, the build pipeline, and the customer roster. The encryption did its job. The access control around everything else did not.

Both of those sentences are true at the same time. If you build things, hold both of them in your head. Design so that a breach still leaves the secrets safe, and then go fix the doors that should never have opened that far in the first place.

title: Headlong: a complete agent harness written in Bash
summary:
Headlong

Most coding agents wake up when you message them, do a job, then stop. Headlong takes the opposite approach. It is a complete agent harness written in Bash, built around shellm, a recursive language model loop that keeps thinking between conversations. Your team's Slack messages arrive as observations in that stream, and the agent decides whether to answer. Each step rebuilds context from an append-only log, recent entries in full and older ones summarised in tiers, so a long-running agent loses nothing to compaction. It is small, readable end to end, and easy to modify. As of 26 November 2026 it has 1,313 stars on GitHub, is Apache-2.0 licensed, and has no GitHub release yet. The repo is now under Laude Institute.

Repo: https://github.com/laude-institute/headlong

What you get

  • A recursive language model loop (shellm) that keeps thinking between conversations, instead of waking up per message
  • Slack messages delivered as observations in the stream, with the agent deciding whether to answer
  • Context rebuilt each step from an append-only log: recent entries in full, older ones summarised in tiers
  • A small Bash codebase, readable end to end and easy to modify

The test for Headlong is a long-running job: does the agent still know what happened last week?

Quick poll

What would you use Headlong for first?

  • Letting it watch a Slack channel
  • Running a long-lived agent on a real repo
  • Reading the Bash source end to end
  • Watching it for now

Vote in the comments.

If you found Headlong interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: How We Built Zero-Upload Passport Photo, Exact-KB PDF & Saudi ZATCA TLV QR Tools 100% in the Browser
summary:
Why do users still have to upload biometric passport selfies, resumes, and tax invoices to unknown cloud servers just to crop a photo to 600x600 (<240KB) or generate a ZATCA QR invoice?

At Diamond Prime Ltd, we built a suite of 200+ privacy-first browser utilities at dprime.org that execute 100% client-side in browser RAM with zero uploads, zero logins, and zero watermarks.

1. Exact-KB Binary Search Compression (HTML5 Canvas)

Government portals like US Visa DS-160 (<= 240KB), Saudi Absher (<= 100KB), and exam portals (<= 50KB) reject images even 1 KB over the limit. Rather than hardcoding quality = 0.7, a 9-step binary search over canvas.toBlob(cb, 'image/jpeg', mid) converges to the maximum quality that stays strictly under the byte limit in ~40ms.

Try it live:

  • Biometric Passport & Visa Photo Studio (14 Country Presets + 4x6 Print Sheet)
  • Exact-KB Image & PDF Compressor (Zero Upload)

2. UTF-8 Safe Saudi ZATCA Phase-1 TLV-Base64 QR Encoding

Arabic business names consume 2 UTF-8 bytes per character. Using TextEncoder guarantees valid TLV byte offsets for Tags 1–5:

const enc = new TextEncoder();
const chunks = [];
for (const [tag, val] of [[1, seller], [2, vatNo], [3, iso], [4, total], [5, vat]]) {
  const bytes = enc.encode(String(val));
  chunks.push(tag, bytes.length, ...bytes);
}
const zatcaBase64 = btoa(String.fromCharCode(...chunks));

For our Visual Height Comparison Simulator (cm & ft/in free) and Official Driving & Aptitude Exam Simulators, we serialize user comparisons and challenge scores directly into location.hash — zero database costs, instant friend sharing, and complete user privacy.

title: I Built Kanbrix, a Self-Hosted Jira Alternative with Rust and React
summary:
What happens when two teammates create an issue in the same project at the same time? Both need a readable key like CORE-42, and each needs a different number.

That’s one of the details behind Kanbrix, an MIT-licensed issue tracker I built for teams that want to run their own Kanban boards, sprint backlogs, and workflows.

Let PostgreSQL assign the issue number

The Rust API uses Axum and SQLx. When it creates an issue, PostgreSQL increments the project's counter and returns the new value in the same statement:

UPDATE projects
SET issue_counter = issue_counter + 1
WHERE id = $1
RETURNING issue_counter;

The increment and the issue insert happen in one transaction. If the insert fails, the counter update rolls back with it. When two requests hit the same project, PostgreSQL serializes their updates to that counter row.

Keep the board current while people work

The frontend is built with React and TypeScript. Dragging a card updates its status or position, and WebSocket events tell other open boards when to refresh. A team can give each project its own workflow columns and plan sprints from the backlog.

The interactive demo starts with three release tasks. Drag Write release notes into In progress to try the basic interaction.

Bring over one Jira project

Kanbrix previews source issues before importing them. You decide how Jira statuses map to Kanbrix columns, then get a report showing what was created, updated, or skipped. Repeating the import into the same destination uses source IDs to update existing issues. Jira rich-text descriptions come across as plain text, so check a few formatting-heavy tickets during your first import. Jira import guide

Run it locally

With Git and Docker Compose installed:

git clone https://github.com/toozuuu/kanbrix.git
cd kanbrix

What happens when two teammates create an issue in the same project at the same time? Both need a readable key like CORE-42, and each needs a different number.

That’s one of the details behind Kanbrix, an MIT-licensed issue tracker I built for teams that want to run their own Kanban boards, sprint backlogs, and workflows.

Let PostgreSQL assign the issue number

The Rust API uses Axum and SQLx. When it creates an issue, PostgreSQL increments the project's counter and returns the new value in the same statement:

UPDATE projects
SET issue_counter = issue_counter + 1
WHERE id = $1
RETURNING issue_counter;

The increment and the issue insert happen in one transaction. If the insert fails, the counter update rolls back with it. When two requests hit the same project, PostgreSQL serializes their updates to that counter row.

Keep the board current while people work

The frontend is built with React and TypeScript. Dragging a card updates its status or position, and WebSocket events tell other open boards when to refresh. A team can give each project its own workflow columns and plan sprints from the backlog.

Kanbrix previews source issues before importing them. You decide how Jira statuses map to Kanbrix columns, then get a report showing what was created, updated, or skipped. title: Create campaign short links from AI with LinkDevi's open-source MCP server
summary:
Creating campaign links often means repeating the same work: add UTMs for each channel, shorten the destinations, generate a QR image, then keep a record of what was created.

We're sharing LinkDevi MCP, an MIT-licensed local connector that exposes that workflow to AI clients supporting MCP over stdio.

Source: https://github.com/kgma-glitch/linkdevi-mcp

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@kgma/linkdevi-mcp

Setup guide: https://linkdevi.com/features/ai

Disclosure: this is our own project, and this article was prepared with AI assistance. The connector code is open source. Using the hosted LinkDevi service requires an account and scoped API key, and your plan's quotas and request limits apply.

What the connector can do

The first release exposes six tools:

Tool Purpose
capabilities Read workspace limits, stored-link usage, granted scopes and metric definitions
preview_campaign Inspect exact UTM destinations and the number of link slots needed
create_campaign Create one saved campaign link per selected channel
list_campaigns Find existing saved campaigns
link_qr Render a PNG QR image for an existing workspace link
campaign_stats Read lifetime recorded redirect counters with explicit limitations

It connects to the same campaign service used by the LinkDevi website. You can return to the website to manage the saved campaign.

1. Install and create a scoped key

You'll need Node.js 22 or newer. Check the package without entering a key:

npx --yes @kgma/linkdevi-mcp@0.1.1 --help

Sign in to LinkDevi, open Connect AI, and create a key with links:read and links:write for the campaign workflow. Use only links:read for a read-only connection.

Keep the real key in your client's protected settings. Don't put it in a prompt, a public configuration file, or a Git commit.

2. Configure your MCP client

For a client using the mcpServers configuration format:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "linkdevi": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["--yes", "@kgma/linkdevi-mcp@0.1.1"],
      "env": {
        "LINKDEVI_API_KEY": "YOUR_SCOPED_KEY",
        "LINKDEVI_BASE_URL": "https://linkdevi.com"
      }
    }
  }
}

Restart the connection after saving. Configuration locations vary by client; it must support launching a local stdio process. The README includes local installation and Windows guidance. This release does not provide a hosted OAuth MCP endpoint.

3. Preview before creating

Try a request such as:

Preview a campaign for https://example.com/sale called December launch, with Facebook, LINE and print channels. Show the exact destinations and quota cost before creating anything.

The AI can check capabilities and call preview_campaign. After you review the result, it can call create_campaign using arguments like these:

{
  "requestId": "a43c37c0-350a-44ef-9d40-a5900c246891",
  "name": "December launch",
  "url": "https://example.com/sale",
  "utmCampaign": "december-launch",
  "domain": "linkdevi.com",
  "channels": ["facebook", "line", "print"]
}

Three channels consume three stored-link slots. A preview does not reserve quota. Supported channels are Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, LINE, email, print, YouTube and X.

Use a new UUID for a new creation intent. If a response is lost, retry with the same requestId and identical payload. Reusing the ID with different content conflicts; the connector does not automatically retry ambiguous requests.

What the counters mean

The campaign report exposes best-effort lifetime redirect counts. They include bots and link previews. They are not unique people, date-based activity, conversions or revenue, and missing channel records are reported as unavailable.

The QR tool renders an image for an existing link using its saved short domain; it does not create a separate saved QR resource.

Running the source tests

Download or clone the public repository, then run:

npm ci
npm test

The tests exercise the official MCP SDK, input validation, retry identity, credential transport restrictions, error handling, and a packed installation running through its actual executable. Fixture tests do not call a model provider or create production customer data.

The connector itself doesn't invoke an LLM. Your chosen AI client's model costs are separate from the LinkDevi service limits.

If you try it, a useful first contribution is a reproducible setup issue or a small improvement to the workflow. Open an issue on GitHub, leaving out real keys and customer data.

title: My AI agents now leave a receipt: an action history for a self-hosted app store
summary:
A few days ago someone on LinkedIn listed six questions every team should answer before building an AI agent. Number 5 was short: "Can you trace what it did?"

I thought my answer was yes. It wasn't.

The setup

I build Agentic App Store, an open-source (MIT) app store you host yourself. You install apps with one click on your own Mac or Linux box, and AI agents can work inside those apps through one door, the AI Hub:

  • Agents like Claude Code or Codex connect to one MCP address and see every installed app's tools.
  • The hub's own assistant can use the same tools from a chat window.
  • Each app marks its tools as read, write or danger. A danger call (delete shapes, replace text) stops in the hub and shows the person a card with Accept / Accept all in this chat / Reject. The prompt never decides that; the hub does.

So the approval part was there. What was missing was the record. The hub kept the last 200 tool calls in memory, without the person's answer, and a restart wiped them.

That's a status page, not a history.

What I wanted to be able to answer

For any AI action, a week later:

  1. When, and through which door (an MCP agent or the assistant chat)?
  2. For whom, which app and tool?
  3. Exactly what the AI sent?
  4. How it ended: done, failed, or never ran?
  5. What the person answered, if the call needed an answer?

Number 4 matters more than I expected. A rejected change never reaches the app, so the app has no record of it. But "the AI tried to delete everything and I said no" is exactly what you want to find later.

The design: one line per call, written where every call passes

Every tool call, from every door, already goes through one function in the hub: calls.call(). That's the natural place to write the history. One JSON line per call, appended to a file in the hub's data folder:

def record(*, via, user, app, tool, kind, args, ok,
           error="", ms=0, approval="", ran=True):
    entry = {
        "id": secrets.token_hex(6),
        "at": time.time(),
        "via": via, "user": user, "app": app, "tool": tool, "kind": kind,
        "args": _args_text(args),      # what the AI sent, cut at 4,000 chars
        "ok": ok, "ran": ran, "error": error[:500], "ms": ms,
        "approval": approval,          # accepted, rejected, allowed, declined, no answer...
    }
    with _lock, _file().open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(entry, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

Plain JSONL on purpose: it's easy to read, easy to back up, and easy to delete. The file keeps the newest 10,000 entries and is readable only by the hub's owner.

Getting the person's answer into the same line

The approval happens in one module (approvals) and the call in another (calls). Both run in the same asyncio task, one tool call at a time, so a ContextVar carries the answer from one to the other without changing every function signature in between:

APPROVAL: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("ai_hub_approval", default="")

# approvals.ask(), after the person clicks Accept:
history.APPROVAL.set("accepted")

# calls.call(), when it writes the line:
approval = history.APPROVAL.get()
history.APPROVAL.set("")   # the answer belongs to this one call only

The reset is important. Without it, the next harmless read in the same chat would show up as "accepted" too.

Calls that never run get their own line with ran: false: rejected changes, reads the person declined, and calls from places that have no chat to ask in (the voice companion, say). Those don't run either. The model is told to ask in the chat.

The bug I found while taking screenshots

I tried it live: I asked the AI to clear a demo drawing and planned to click Reject for the screenshot. I was too slow. Claude Code gave up waiting for the tool call before the hub's own 4-minute timeout, and the history showed... nothing for that call.

When the client gives up, the hub's waiting coroutine gets cancelled. My code only wrote a line after a decision, and a cancellation is not a decision. So "never asked" and "asked, but nobody answered" looked the same, which is exactly the gap the history was supposed to close.

The fix is small:

async def _kept_answer(tool, args, user, via, chat, post, card, waiting):
    try:
        return await _answer(chat, post, card, waiting)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        history.record(..., ok=False, ran=False,
                       approval="no answer: the AI stopped waiting")
        raise

Record, then re-raise: the cancellation still does what it should, and the history keeps the attempt. There's a test for it now too.

What the owner sees

On the hub page, the old "Recent tool calls" card became History of the AI's actions:

  • Search across everything (an app, a tool, a person, words the AI sent, "rejected").
  • Click a row to see the whole entry, and delete it if you want.
  • Delete all, after a question that says how many entries will go.
  • Download the whole history as JSON.
  • Times show in your browser's time zone (the containers run on UTC).

Only the hub's owner can see it, because an entry holds whatever the AI sent, and that can be anyone's data.

What it is, and what it isn't

It is the everyday kind of audit trail: on your own server, next to your data, covering every agent that goes through the hub.

It is not a validated compliance system. If you work in a regulated field, the hub's history can support your own validation, but it doesn't replace it.

Try it

Agentic App Store is open source (MIT): https://about.reflex-ddns.com

If you run agents against real systems, I'm curious: who reviews what your agents did last week, and where do they look?

title: Self-Hosted Zero Trust – A Journey, Not a Masterclass
summary:
Self-Hosted Zero Trust – A Journey, Not a Masterclass

Part 1 – How I ended up running Pangolin, CrowdSec and k3s

I've been working in IT for more than 35 years, and somehow it still hasn't stopped being a hobby. My homelab is probably the best evidence of that.

What started as a simple self-hosted environment has gradually turned into something more interesting: a combination of Pangolin, Traefik, CrowdSec and k3s, running on a relatively inexpensive VPS and connected to services in my home network.

Getting there wasn't always easy. Some things worked surprisingly well. Others kept me busy for evenings that I had originally planned to spend doing something completely different. If you run a homelab, you probably know the feeling.

This is the first in a series of articles about that journey. It's not a reference architecture, and it certainly isn't a Kubernetes masterclass. I simply want to share some of the things I've learned along the way, including the mistakes.

The problem with exposing services

Running a service at home is easy enough these days. A container, a volume, a few environment variables, and you're usually up and running.

Making that service available from outside your network is where things get interesting. For years, the usual approach was something like this:

  • Forward a port on your router.
  • Set up a reverse proxy.
  • Get a TLS certificate.
  • Add authentication if the application needs it.

And it works. But as the number of services grows, so does the number of things you need to maintain and protect.

What happens if an application has an authentication vulnerability? What about an administration interface that was never really intended to face the internet? And how much unwanted traffic is reaching those services in the first place?

I wanted an alternative that wouldn't require opening incoming ports at home for the applications I wanted to access remotely. I also didn't want to connect to a conventional VPN every time I needed to access a web application.

That's where Pangolin came into the picture.

Enter Pangolin

Pangolin is a self-hosted remote access platform built around tunnels, identity-aware access and a reverse proxy.

The idea is simple. You run a gateway on a publicly reachable machine, and a connector inside your private network establishes an outbound connection to it. Your applications stay where they are.

In my case, the picture looks like this:

                        Internet
                            |
            Public VPS (k3s)
     +-----------------------------------------+
     | Traefik <-> CrowdSec + AppSec           |
     | Pangolin                                |
     | Gerbil                                  |
     | Forgejo, inbuxa                         |
     +-----------------------------------------+
                            ^
                            |
              WireGuard tunnel (outbound from home)
                            |
                     +-------------+
                     |    Newt     |
                     +-------------+
                            |
                      Home network
                            |
                   Private applications

Newt establishes the tunnel from inside the network. There's no need to forward incoming ports on the home router for these tunneled resources. For this setup, the public HTTPS and tunnel endpoints live on the VPS, not at home.

Depending on the application, I can decide whether it should be publicly accessible, require authentication at the gateway or remain a private resource. For web applications exposed through the gateway, a browser is enough. For private network resources, Pangolin also offers a client – but that's not something I need for every web application.

That distinction matters. My Git server, for example, has different requirements from an internal administration interface. Treating every application in exactly the same way would make the system either unnecessarily restrictive or unnecessarily exposed.

A word on "Zero Trust"

I use the term in a practical sense, not as a NIST 800-207 checklist. No application is trusted just because a request comes from a particular network. Each resource gets its own access policy, and none of my remotely exposed homelab services require incoming ports to be opened on my home router.

It isn't perfect. The VPS terminates TLS, so it's a component I have to trust – and so is the provider it runs on. Being clear about where trust remains is, I think, more useful than pretending there is none.

A gateway is not a complete security solution

Pangolin solved an important part of the problem for me, but it didn't make unwanted internet traffic disappear. Public services still attract scanners, crawlers, bots and automated exploitation attempts.

Anyone who has looked through reverse proxy logs on a public server will recognise this:

GET /.env
GET /.git/config
GET /wp-login.php
GET /xmlrpc.php

It doesn't particularly matter whether you're running WordPress. Someone will still come looking for it.

Most of these requests are simply background noise on today's internet. Some are attempts to exploit known vulnerabilities. Either way, I'd rather not have my applications spend resources dealing with them.

That's why I added CrowdSec. CrowdSec analyses logs, identifies suspicious behaviour and shares threat intelligence. Its enforcement components, called bouncers, then act on the resulting security decisions.

Later, I added CrowdSec AppSec, which inspects HTTP requests before they reach an application. The two approaches complement each other: one looks at behaviour and reputation, the other examines the request itself.

But there's an important distinction I didn't fully appreciate at the beginning: blocking a malicious request and banning an IP address are not necessarily the same thing.

I've been working in IT for more than 35 years, and somehow it still hasn't stopped being a hobby. My homelab is probably the best evidence of that.

The problem with exposing services

Running a service at home is easy enough these days. A container, a volume, a few environment variables, and you're usually up and running.

Making that service available from outside your network is where things get interesting. For years, the usual approach was something like this:

  • Forward a port on your router.
  • Set up a reverse proxy.
  • Get a TLS certificate.
  • Add authentication if the application needs it.

And it works. But as the number of services grows, so does the number of things you need to maintain and protect.

I wanted an alternative that wouldn't require opening incoming ports at home for the applications I wanted to access remotely. I also didn't want to connect to a conventional VPN every time I needed to access a web application.

That's where Pangolin came into the picture.

Enter Pangolin

Pangolin is a self-hosted remote access platform built around tunnels, identity-aware access and a reverse proxy.

The idea is simple. You run a gateway on a publicly reachable machine, and a connector inside your private network establishes an outbound connection to it. Your applications stay where they are.

In my case, the picture looks like this:

                        Internet
                            |
            Public VPS (k3s)
     +-----------------------------------------+
     | Traefik <-> CrowdSec + AppSec           |
     | Pangolin                                |
     | Gerbil                                  |
     | Forgejo, inbuxa                         |
     +-----------------------------------------+
                            ^
                            |
              WireGuard tunnel (outbound from home)
                            |
                     +-------------+
                     |    Newt     |
                     +-------------+
                            |
                      Home network
                            |
                   Private applications

Newt establishes the tunnel from inside the network. There's no need to forward incoming ports on the home router for these tunneled resources. For this setup, the public HTTPS and tunnel endpoints live on the VPS, not at home.

GET /.git/config
GET /wp-login.php
GET /xmlrpc.php

It doesn't particularly matter whether you're running WordPress. Someone will still come looking for it.

title: Three things I fixed so my terminal AI agent stops making me wait
summary:
I've been building Tango, an open-source agent harness that runs in the terminal. You talk to it, it reads files, runs commands, and edits code. Using it every day, I found that the things that annoyed me most weren't about the model. They were the moments where either the agent or I was stuck waiting.

Here are three fixes, with screenshots from a small demo project (a Rust + SQLite expense ledger). In the first two sections the model's replies are scripted so the demo is repeatable; the UI and tools are real. The third section is a real reply from glm-5.4. Many of the TUI's labels and key hints are in Chinese, which is why some text in the screenshots looks unfamiliar.

1. Starting a dev server no longer blocks the turn

Ask an agent to run npm run dev and the bash tool waits for a command that never exits, until the 120-second timeout kills it. For those two minutes the agent can't do anything else.

Tango's bash tool now takes background: true. The command starts detached in its own process group. Tango waits about 2 seconds to catch commands that fail right away (port in use, typo), then returns an id like p1 with the pid and the first lines of output. The turn keeps going.

Three tools manage it afterwards:

tool what it does
process_logs last N lines of output plus state (running 6s, exited 1, killed)
process_stop SIGTERM to the process group, SIGKILL 3 s later if it's still alive
process_list every background process this Tango started

Limits: at most 8 at a time, each keeps the last 200,000 characters of output, and all of them are killed when Tango exits. Read-only mode refuses them.

2. Typing while the agent is busy

When the agent is mid-task and I think of the next thing, I used to either wait or press Ctrl+C and restate both requests.

Now Enter during a turn queues the prompt. Queued prompts go out in order when the turn ends.

/queue opens the queue: d deletes an item, Enter merges the selected one into the running turn, a merges all, c clears.

If I forgot a detail ("round amounts to two decimals"), Alt+Enter adds the text to the running turn instead of queueing it; the model sees it on its next request. Ctrl+C stops the current reply and keeps the queue. If you want every busy Enter to work like Alt+Enter, run /queue auto append.

3. Using a new model the day it ships

When Zhipu's GLM Coding Plan started serving glm-5.4, I added it as zhipu-plan/glm-5.4. It speaks the Anthropic protocol and reads its key from ZHIPU_CODING_PLAN_API_KEY.

/model opens the picker. Typing filters it, Enter switches and saves the choice as the default. Model ids match fuzzily everywhere (case-insensitive subsequence), so glm54 finds it, and tango -m glm54 uses it for one run only.

I asked it, in Chinese, to sum up this month's spending in one sentence. It listed the directory, found ledger.db, queried and summed the entries, and answered: ¥799.30 across 7 entries, half of it on one ¥399 mechanical keyboard. This screenshot is unedited model output.

Trying it

Tango is MIT-licensed. It's China-first (DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, and GLM work with one API key on mainland endpoints, no proxy), and it also has presets for Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, xAI, OpenRouter, and a local model. It installs from source for now: Node 20+ for the core and Rust for the TUI. Steps are in the README: https://github.com/cnshsliu/tango

I'd like to hear what makes you wait when you use a coding agent. That's the list I work from.
